name: Big Apple

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the early 1930s at the Big Apple Night Club in Columbia, South Carolina.
It was later popularized by university students and professional dance troupes, eventually becoming a national craze in 1937.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance was a social activity meant for group enjoyment.
It served as a 'pepper-upper' at parties and was used as a performance piece in theaters.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: File:"Big Apple" routine at Lindy on the Rocks 2024.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/95/%22Big_Apple%22_routine_at_Lindy_on_the_Rocks_2024.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in a circle with participants facing the center.
A leader calls out steps, and individual couples ('shiners') take turns performing in the center.
The dance is highly improvisational and uses 8-count patterns.
Watch for Susie Q, Truckin, Shorty George.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (H1K5M5xluZs)
Captions name each signature move as it appears

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The Big Apple is danced to swing music.
The rhythm is fast-paced and energetic, requiring dancers to keep up with the tempo of the jazz band.
Listen for the Brass, Woodwinds, Percussion, Piano.
The pulse is 4/4.
Fast-paced, high-energy swing music characterized by a driving beat that supports vigorous, improvisational dance movements.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Frankie Manning, Betty Wood, Billy Spivey, Donald Davis, Harold 'Goo-Goo' Wiles, Frank 'Fat Sam' Boyd.
The 'Little Apple' is a variation involving fewer dancers, where participants take turns grabbing a partner to dance in the center of the circle.
The Big Apple is closely related to the Lindy Hop, Charleston, Black Bottom, and the Shag, sharing a common improvisational spirit and jazz-based movement.

It should sound like this: Fast-paced, high-energy swing music characterized by a driving beat that supports vigorous, improvisational dance movements.
